opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the appeal of know-your-customer checks comes down to a simple observation: almost every dangerous capability, whether it's a frontier AI model or a benchtop DNA synthesizer, is delivered to people through a relatively small number of chokepoints. Customers rent cloud compute from a handful of providers, access frontier models through a few APIs, and order synthetic DNA from a limited set of companies. Those chokepoints are already commercial relationships, and commercial relationships come with a natural moment where you can ask, "Who are you, and what are you trying to do?"

We have a long track record with this in finance. Banks verify identities, flag suspicious patterns, and file reports, not because every customer is a criminal, but because anonymity at scale makes it very easy for the small fraction of bad actors to hide. KYC doesn't stop all money laundering, but it raises the cost, creates an audit trail, and gives investigators something to work with afterward. I think the same logic transfers quite well to AI and biology.

What makes it promising, rather than just plausible, is a few things. First, it targets the actor rather than the technology itself. You don't have to cripple a model or ban a class of research to manage misuse risk. You can let legitimate researchers, companies, and clinicians have broad access while being more careful about anonymous or unverifiable users seeking the most sensitive capabilities. That's a much better trade-off than blanket restrictions, which tend to punish beneficial use and push activity toward less accountable providers.

Second, it enables tiered access. Not everything needs the same scrutiny. Most uses of a chatbot or most gene orders are completely benign. But if you know who your customer is, you can reserve higher-risk capabilities, like detailed help with pathogen enhancement or large-scale compute for training very capable systems, for verified institutions with a legitimate need. Without identity, you can't really have tiers. You just have one door that's either open or shut.

Third, it creates accountability and deterrence. If someone knows their request is tied to a verified identity, that alone changes behavior. And if something does go wrong, there's a trail to follow, which matters for both enforcement and learning from incidents.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. KYC has real weaknesses. Identities can be faked or borrowed, shell companies exist, and determined state actors can work around it. There are also legitimate concerns about privacy and about locking out researchers in countries with weaker institutional infrastructure. So the design matters a lot: how much verification, at which thresholds, who holds the data, and how it's coordinated across providers so that a bad actor refused by one company can't simply walk next door. That last point is crucial, because KYC only works if the chokepoint is actually a chokepoint and not one of many open doors.

But as a layer in a broader defense-in-depth strategy, alongside model safeguards, sequence screening, and monitoring, I think it's one of the most practical, near-term tools we have. It builds on infrastructure and norms that already exist, it's relatively cheap compared to the risks, and it scales with the capability: the more dangerous the thing, the more confident you want to be about who's on the other end.

r001.rationale: The response says providers can ask who a customer is and what they are trying to do, and describes reserving sensitive capabilities for verified users with a legitimate need.

r002.rationale: It does not mention LLM-assisted information gathering or reducing the effort needed for KYC due diligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose adapting KYC methods from nucleic acid synthesis screening to powerful AI model access.

r004.rationale: It does not argue that labor-intensive due diligence makes trusted-partner programs impractical as a long-term general solution.

r005.rationale: It does not specify that a human makes the final access decision in an LLM-assisted KYC workflow.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the reason I keep coming back to know-your-customer is that it's one of the few governance tools that actually sits at a real chokepoint, rather than trying to police the whole landscape after the fact.

If you think about where the dangerous capability actually lives in biology, a huge amount of it is concentrated in a small number of service providers. Gene synthesis companies, the firms that will build you a plasmid or a cell line, cloud labs, and increasingly the labs and companies offering the most capable AI models through an API. Those are points where someone has to actually hand over something physical or grant access to something computational. That's a very different situation from, say, trying to stop information from spreading, which is basically hopeless once it's out.

And KYC is a mature idea. We've been doing it in finance for decades. Banks have to know who they're dealing with, verify identities, understand what a customer is plausibly doing, flag things that don't fit. It's not perfect, but it raised the cost of money laundering substantially and it did so without shutting down banking for ordinary people. The logic transfers quite directly. If you want to order a long synthetic DNA sequence that encodes something worrying, or you want to run a model at the kind of scale and with the kind of fine-tuning access that could meaningfully uplift a bioweapons effort, it's reasonable to ask who you are and whether that request makes sense for you.

What I like about it is that it's proportionate. You're not banning the technology. A legitimate vaccine researcher at a university or a biotech company has nothing to hide and can be verified fairly easily. The person you're actually worried about, who doesn't have an institutional affiliation, who can't explain why they need this, who's trying to break up an order into smaller pieces across several suppliers, that's exactly the profile that KYC is designed to surface.

I'd also say it's good because it creates a paper trail and it creates accountability. Right now, a lot of synthesis screening is voluntary, and the providers that do it well are essentially subsidising safety for everyone while competing against those that don't. Mandatory KYC levels the playing field and gives us a record if something goes wrong.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. KYC can be evaded, it imposes costs, and for AI in particular there are open questions about what the right verification tier looks like and how you handle open-weight models where there's no customer to know. But as part of a layered defence, alongside sequence screening, model evaluations, and attribution capabilities, I think it's one of the most practical and least controversial things we can actually implement in the next couple of years.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss LLM-assisted information gathering or how that could reduce KYC due-diligence effort.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that you don’t necessarily have to control every piece of information. You can focus on the points where someone gets access to a capability. Knowing how to do something and being able to do it are different things, and access to a powerful AI system or a service that synthesizes DNA can help bridge that gap.

Know-your-customer checks give the provider a chance to ask: Who is requesting this? Are they actually who they say they are? And does the request make sense in the context of their work? For DNA synthesis, that can complement screening the sequence itself. For powerful AI, it could mean additional checks before granting access to particularly sensitive capabilities.

It also creates accountability. If access is tied to a verified identity, it becomes harder to evade a restriction simply by opening another account, and there’s a better basis for investigating misuse.

Of course, identity verification doesn’t tell you someone’s intentions. A legitimate customer can act maliciously, and identities can be stolen. So I’d see this as one layer alongside technical safeguards and screening of requests. The promising part is that it gives us a practical intervention at the point of access, while allowing most legitimate research and use to continue.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that you can make a capability widely useful without making it anonymously available to absolutely anyone. Know-your-customer checks give the provider some understanding of who is requesting access, and potentially what they intend to do with it.

In biology, you might apply that when someone orders synthetic DNA. With powerful AI, you might apply it when someone requests access to capabilities that could substantially assist with dangerous biological work. In both cases, there’s an opportunity to ask: Who is this customer? Is this request consistent with a legitimate use? Does it warrant further scrutiny?

That’s promising because you’re intervening at a point where a provider can actually make a decision about access. You don’t have to solve the much harder problem of monitoring everything someone does afterward. And identity checks can create accountability and make it harder to evade restrictions simply by opening another account.

Of course, knowing someone’s identity doesn’t establish that their intentions are good. So I would see this as one layer of protection, alongside assessing the request itself, securing the service, and having a process for responding to suspicious activity. The challenge is to make those checks proportionate to the capability and the risk, while preserving access for legitimate users.
